accepted.question_text: Let f : R^n -> R^m be a function that is Lipschitz continuous near a point x_bar, and assume every matrix in Clarke's generalized Jacobian of f at x_bar is surjective. If y_bar = f(x_bar), must there exist a continuous local selection s of the inverse image mapping f^{-1} near y_bar such that s(y_bar) = x_bar and s is calm at y_bar, meaning that for some constant gamma > 0 one has ||s(y) - x_bar|| <= gamma ||y - y_bar|| for all nearby y?

evidence.quote: Here is the open problem: Conjecture. Consider a function f : Rn -> Rm which is Lipschitz continuous around x_bar and suppose that all matrices A in Clarke's generalized Jacobian of f at x_bar are surjective. Then f^{-1} has a continuous local selection around y_bar for x_bar which is calm at y_bar = f(x_bar).

accepted.question_text: Is every 6-dimensional polytope 3-linked, in the sense that for every choice of three pairs of distinct vertices there exist three pairwise disjoint paths in its graph, each connecting one chosen pair?

evidence.quote: A graph G is k-linked if for any selection of k pairs of all distinct vertices Y := {(s1,t1),..., (sk,tk)}, (k >= 1) there exist k disjoint paths, connecting the k pairs of points in Y. If the graph of a polytope is k-linked we say that the polytope is also k-linked.
The remaining question is that if all the 6-polytopes are 3-linked.

accepted.question_text: Does the combinatorial 3-polytope FFS3 admit a decomposable geometric realization, where decomposable means representable as a Minkowski sum of two convex bodies that are not similar to one another? Equivalently, is every geometric realization of FFS3 indecomposable?

evidence.quote: A polytope is called decomposable [20] if it can be represented as Minkowski sum of dis-similar convex bodies.
The only remaining case is the (combinatorial) polytope FFS3 with its graph shown in Fig. 1. It is conjectured that this polytope has no decomposable geometric realisation.

accepted.question_text: Let C_1 and C_2 be compact convex sets in a Hilbert space H. Must there exist a point x in H such that, if p_i is a projection of x onto C_i for i in {1,2}, then the normal vector x - p_i defines a supporting hyperplane that strongly exposes the singleton face {p_i} of C_i? Here a point p in a convex set C is strongly exposed by a linear functional f when f(p) = sup_{x in C} f(x) and every sequence (x_k) in C with f(x_k) approaching sup_{x in C} f(x) converges to p.

evidence.quote: The conjecture states that there always exists a point x in H such that for each of its projections p_i onto C_i, i in {1,2} the relevant normals x-p_1 and x-p_2 define the hyperplanes that strongly expose the faces {p_1} and {p_2} of C_1 and C_2 respectively.

Recall (see [15, Definition 8.27]) that a point x in C is strongly exposed by a linear functional f if f(x) = sup_{x' in C} f(x') and x_k -> x for all sequences {x_k} subset C such that lim f(x_k) = sup_{x in C} f(x).

accepted.question_text: For nonconvex feasibility problems A intersection B != emptyset involving proximal sets, what can be proved about the dynamics and convergence of the continuous-time Douglas-Rachford flow associated with the operator T(x) = (lambda (2P_B - Id)(2P_A - Id) + (1 - lambda) Id)x in the limit lambda -> 0^+, especially in settings such as a subtransversal ellipse and a line or a p-sphere and a line where the discrete Douglas-Rachford method has complicated global behavior?

evidence.quote: For the feasibility problem of finding a point in the nonempty intersection A intersection B != emptyset of proximal sets A and B, the Douglas-Rachford method for a given starting point x_0 generates a sequence x_n in T x_{n-1} := (lambda(2P_B - Id)(2P_A - Id) + (1-lambda)Id) x_{n-1} where P_A, P_B denote the usual projection operators for A, B respectively and lambda in (0,1] is usually taken to be 1/2.
Veit Elser has suggested analysing the continuous time version of the method in these more general settings and has generously furnished the images in Figure 5.

accepted.question_text: Given points a_1, ..., a_m in a Euclidean space X, can one write an explicit and neat formula or characterization for the unique minimizer of min_{x in X} max_{i in {1, ..., m}} ||a_i - x||, that is, for the center of the smallest Euclidean sphere containing all the points? More generally, what analogous description is available when X is an arbitrary normed or metric space, or when the maximum over the m distances is replaced by an arbitrary norm on R^m?

evidence.quote: Given a finite set of points a_1,...,a_m in X, where X is an Euclidean space, find the solution to the problem min_{x in X} max_{i in {1,...,m}} ||a_i - x||.

The problem has a unique solution for which x is the centre of the minimal Euclidean sphere that contains all points. However it is unclear whether there exists a neat way to write this explicitly. This is a particular case of a more general problem.

accepted.question_text: Let Omega be a finite family of convex polytopes in R^n. For each unit vector g in S^{n-1}, define C(g) to be the convex hull of all support faces Arg max_{x in P} <x,g> taken over P in Omega, and define F(Omega) = {C(g) : g in S^{n-1}}. Starting from Omega_0, iterate Omega_i = F(Omega_{i-1}). Which initial finite families Omega_0 have the property that this sequence eventually enters a 2-cycle, meaning that there exists N with Omega_{N+2} = Omega_N?

evidence.quote: Given a finite family Omega of convex polytopes in R^n, for each unit vector g in S^{n-1} we construct a new polytope as the convex hull of all support faces of all polytopes in the family Omega, i.e. we define the function C(g) := conv {Arg max_{x in P} <x,g> | P in Omega}. Collecting all such polytopes, we obtain a new finite family of polytopes, F(Omega) = {C(g) g in S^{n-1}}.
Since we now know that the conjecture is false, the question is to find a characterisation of such collections of polytopes that yield two-cycles, extending and generalising the results of [9, 23].

accepted.question_text: Does every convex 3-polytope admit a nonoverlapping net, that is, can one cut the polytope along some collection of edges so that the resulting connected surface unfolds into the plane without self-overlap?

evidence.quote: A net (or unfolding) of a 3-polytope is the process of cutting it along its edges, so that the resulting connected shape can be flattened (developed) into the plane.
The Durer's conjecture is a claim that any polytope has a nonoverlapping net.
